features.name: Inline locale switch
features.description: The ship-to banner becomes a control rather than an announcement: country and currency change in place and every price on the page re-renders without leaving it.
features.hmw: How might we let someone act on a storefront's assumption about where they are, at the moment that assumption changes what they see?

features.name: Dual-currency price line
features.description: Every price carries both the storefront currency and the detected-locale currency, so there is nothing to switch and no ambiguity to resolve later.
features.hmw: How might we let someone act on a storefront's assumption about where they are, at the moment that assumption changes what they see?

features.name: Locale settled at entry
features.description: The storefront asks once, before any results exist, and never re-asks — moving the decision ahead of the screens that would otherwise inherit the ambiguity.
features.hmw: How might we let someone act on a storefront's assumption about where they are, at the moment that assumption changes what they see?

features.name: Compare tray
features.description: Pin up to four results and see them side by side on specs, rating volume, and delivered price, without ever leaving the results page.
features.hmw: How might we help a shopper reach one defensible choice without leaving the results in order to compare them?

features.name: Deciding facts on the row
features.description: Rating count, recent purchase volume, and variant depth surface on the result row itself, so comparison never needs a second screen at all.
features.hmw: How might we help a shopper reach one defensible choice without leaving the results in order to compare them?

features.name: Badge provenance
features.description: Tapping any authority badge says what it certifies, over what window, and against which set of products.
features.hmw: How might we make competing trust signals mean something a shopper can actually weigh against each other?

features.name: One ranked answer, shown its work
features.description: A single top recommendation per query that states the two facts it won on, replacing the competing badges with one accountable pick.
features.hmw: How might we make competing trust signals mean something a shopper can actually weigh against each other?

features.name: Add the default variant from results
features.description: Listings with a sensible default offer get a direct add control on the row; multi-variant listings get an inline picker instead of a page hop.
features.hmw: How might we keep the effort of reaching a cart from deciding which product wins?

features.name: Variant depth shown before the click
features.description: A listing declares how many choices stand between the shopper and a cart, so effort is visible while comparing rather than discovered afterwards.
features.hmw: How might we keep the effort of reaching a cart from deciding which product wins?

features.name: Persistent add bar
features.description: The add-to-cart control is pinned within reach at every scroll position, with the checkout shortcut demoted out of accidental range.
features.hmw: How might we make sure the action a shopper came to take is never the hardest one to find?

features.name: Confirmation that survives the scroll
features.description: The added state persists as a bar carrying the running subtotal and an undo, rather than a banner that disappears on its own.
features.hmw: How might we make sure the action a shopper came to take is never the hardest one to find?

design_directions.name: Decide in the Grid
design_directions.summary: The product page is the bottleneck, not the catalogue. Everything needed to choose between options and to add one of them belongs in the results list, so a shopper who knows the category never has to open a product page at all.
design_directions.differentiator: Collapses comparison and the add action into a single surface — the only direction where a successful session never leaves the results page.
hmws_addressed: How might we help a shopper reach one defensible choice without leaving the results in order to compare them?
How might we keep the effort of reaching a cart from deciding which product wins?
design_directions.tradeoff: The result row gets dense fast, and products that genuinely need explaining — variants, sizing, compatibility — are under-served by a row. It also gives up whatever persuasion the product page was doing, on the assumption it was doing none.

design_directions.name: One Answer, Shown Its Work
design_directions.summary: Shoppers in a generic category do not want to compare; they want a pick they can defend. The system takes the ranking decision and earns the right to it by exposing the evidence behind every recommendation.
design_directions.differentiator: Replaces competing authority badges with one accountable recommendation and the reasoning it rests on — the only direction that moves the decision from the shopper to the system.
hmws_addressed: How might we help a shopper reach one defensible choice without leaving the results in order to compare them?
How might we make competing trust signals mean something a shopper can actually weigh against each other?
design_directions.tradeoff: An enormous trust burden concentrated in one place: a single bad top pick poisons the whole surface, and there is no cheap way to recover it. Shoppers who came to browse lose the browse.

design_directions.name: Never Lose the Thread
design_directions.summary: The shopping model is fine; the continuity around it is broken. Fix the four moments where the interface drops the shopper — the silent locale swap, the dead Enter key, the clipped primary action, the vanishing confirmation — and the existing flow works.
design_directions.differentiator: Touches only state, context, and reachability. It is the one direction that changes no ranking, no comparison, and no merchandising.
hmws_addressed: How might we let someone act on a storefront's assumption about where they are, at the moment that assumption changes what they see?
How might we make sure the action a shopper came to take is never the hardest one to find?
design_directions.tradeoff: Deliberately declines the ten-thousand-results decision problem, which is the highest drop-off stage in the journey. It makes a frustrating flow smooth without making a hard choice easier.
